title: No Reservations
full_review:
Very nearly on a par with the delightful 2001 German film "Mostly Martha," on which it is based, "No Reservations" (Warner Bros.) scores as the very sweet, engaging story of a woman who learns to open herself up to life.

Now set in New York, the film focuses on utterly work-obsessed master chef Kate (Catherine Zeta-Jones), who rules the kitchen of the trendy (fictional) Greenwich Village eatery run by Paula (Patricia Clarkson).

Kate is so rigid that Paula has insisted she see a therapist (Bob Balaban) or else, but Kate monopolizes her sessions, paying little heed to the therapist's insights and often ending their time together by cooking him a gourmet meal.

When her sister is killed in a car crash, Kate learns that her sister's wish was that she take care of her 9-year-old daughter, Zoe (Abigail Breslin), much to Kate's chagrin, as she cares for the child but has no idea how to communicate with the sad little girl. And Zoe would much rather eat the kid-friendly food she remembers her mother giving her than Kate's carefully prepared gourmet dishes -- fish heads and all.

While Kate deals with her grief and her new charge, Paula hires happy-go-lucky, opera-loving sous-chef Nick (Aaron Eckhart) who becomes a favorite of the kitchen staff and customers.

For his part, he feels honored to be in the same kitchen as Kate, whom he has admired for her culinary prowess, but she perceives him as a rival. However, after Kate decides to bring Zoe to the restaurant rather than entrust her to an unreliable baby sitter, Nick quickly wins the girl over, and in one of the film's most heartwarming scenes, gently encourages the girl to eat his spaghetti, thereby eroding Kate's distrust and winning her grudging admiration.

Eventually Zoe, Cupid-like, contrives to bring the couple closer together. This is one of the rare films where, refreshingly, a romantically smitten couple doesn't jump into bed, at least not at first, and when they do, it's only implied. But later, when Kate and Nick have a falling out, the perceptive Zoe offers one of her dolls for the apparently lonely Kate to sleep with, a touchingly intended but, it must be said, morally dubious little scene.

Despite some formulaic and overly sentimental moments, director Scott Hicks maintains a reasonably realistic tone, allowing the engaging story to unfold at an unhurried pace, while the performances are immensely appealing. Zeta-Jones is all brisk efficiency in the kitchen, but delineates the lonely person underneath. Breslin is convincing as the bereaved child, wise beyond her years. And Eckhart, though almost too perfectly agreeable as written, makes a persuasive leading man.

Notwithstanding the flagged elements below, "No Reservations" registers as a good, old-fashioned romantic comedy. Hot on the heels of "Ratatouille," the movie makes this a good season for food movies.

Apart from a handful of expletives and crass expressions, including an instance of profanity and some remarks that imply the acceptability of premarital living arrangements, and one such implied encounter, the film may be acceptable for older adolescents. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
